**Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. ONE exception, and only one: a \`plan-review\` that recorded **Request Changes** or **Needs Discussion** makes the plan's deliverable un-settled again, so the revision pass it names IS a \`plan\` that is still owed — see the plan-review gate immediately below, which bounds it to a single cycle.

**Before routing on session-fit, check whether a \`plan-review\` is due (the plan-review gate).** A plan on record is not automatically ready to build against. Recommend \`plan-review\` when ALL of these hold: a plan exists; the gate is met; and NO plan-review verdict is on the trail yet. **The gate is met** when the plan says so itself ("plan-review due: yes", the answer the plan phase is instructed to record) or when, reading the plan, any of these is true: (a) the session-fit answer is "needs multiple sessions"; (b) it names a routed-around contract gap with a ticket identifier (as opposed to an explicit "none identified"); (c) any step relaxes a validation, a contract, or a guard — a widened input, a dropped check, a softened assertion, a gate turned advisory; (d) it touches credential, merge-rule, or dispatch-contract surfaces. **When none of (a)–(d) holds, do NOT emit \`plan-review\`** — fall straight through to the session-fit routing below, exactly as before this gate existed. The step is gated, not universal: it exists to protect the throughput of the work that needs it, so a clean small plan must reach \`implementation\` with no extra dispatch, and a plan's own "plan-review due: no" is taken at face value unless the plan visibly contradicts it (a named routed-around gap sitting beside a "no" is the contradiction to act on).
**Once a plan-review verdict IS on the trail, route on the verdict — and bound the loop at one cycle:**

- **Approve** → route on the session-fit answer exactly as today ("fits one session" → \`implementation\`, "needs multiple sessions" → \`breakdown\`). Do NOT re-emit \`plan-review\` on a plan that already has one; and note that this Approve authorizes implementation only — it is never close-out evidence (see the close-out rules in Step 0 and above).

- **Request Changes / Needs Discussion (the first one)** → \`plan\` — the revision pass, which reads the verdict and answers each finding. This is the single exception to "Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb" above.

- **A SECOND Request Changes / Needs Discussion on the same task** → **stop and escalate to the human edge: recommend \`blocked\`**, naming the findings that survived two passes and what decision is needed. One revision cycle (plan → plan-review → revised plan → plan-review) is *converging*; a second is *looping*, and looping is not fixed by another pass. Do NOT emit a third \`plan-review\`, and do NOT emit another \`plan\`.

**Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. ONE exception, and only one: a \`plan-review\` that recorded **Request Changes** or **Needs Discussion** makes the plan's deliverable un-settled again, so the revision pass it names IS a \`plan\` that is still owed — see the plan-review gate immediately below, which bounds it to a single cycle.

**Before routing on session-fit, check whether a \`plan-review\` is due (the plan-review gate).** A plan on record is not automatically ready to build against. Recommend \`plan-review\` when ALL of these hold: a plan exists; the gate is met; and NO plan-review verdict is on the trail yet. **The gate is met** when the plan says so itself ("plan-review due: yes", the answer the plan phase is instructed to record) or when, reading the plan, any of these is true: (a) the session-fit answer is "needs multiple sessions"; (b) it names a routed-around contract gap with a ticket identifier (as opposed to an explicit "none identified"); (c) any step relaxes a validation, a contract, or a guard — a widened input, a dropped check, a softened assertion, a gate turned advisory; (d) it touches credential, merge-rule, or dispatch-contract surfaces. **When none of (a)–(d) holds, do NOT emit \`plan-review\`** — fall straight through to the session-fit routing below, exactly as before this gate existed. The step is gated, not universal: it exists to protect the throughput of the work that needs it, so a clean small plan must reach \`implementation\` with no extra dispatch, and a plan's own "plan-review due: no" is taken at face value unless the plan visibly contradicts it (a named routed-around gap sitting beside a "no" is the contradiction to act on).
**Once a plan-review verdict IS on the trail, route on the verdict — and bound the loop at one cycle:**

- **Approve** → route on the session-fit answer exactly as today ("fits one session" → \`implementation\`, "needs multiple sessions" → \`breakdown\`). Do NOT re-emit \`plan-review\` on a plan that already has one; and note that this Approve authorizes implementation only — it is never close-out evidence (see the close-out rules in Step 0 and above).

- **Request Changes / Needs Discussion (the first one)** → \`plan\` — the revision pass, which reads the verdict and answers each finding. This is the single exception to "Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb" above.

- **A SECOND Request Changes / Needs Discussion on the same task** → **stop and escalate to the human edge: recommend \`blocked\`**, naming the findings that survived two passes and what decision is needed. One revision cycle (plan → plan-review → revised plan → plan-review) is *converging*; a second is *looping*, and looping is not fixed by another pass. Do NOT emit a third \`plan-review\`, and do NOT emit another \`plan\`.

**Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. ONE exception, and only one: a \`plan-review\` that recorded **Request Changes** or **Needs Discussion** makes the plan's deliverable un-settled again, so the revision pass it names IS a \`plan\` that is still owed — see the plan-review gate immediately below, which bounds it to a single cycle.

**Before routing on session-fit, check whether a \`plan-review\` is due (the plan-review gate).** A plan on record is not automatically ready to build against. Recommend \`plan-review\` when ALL of these hold: a plan exists; the gate is met; and NO plan-review verdict is on the trail yet. **The gate is met** when the plan says so itself ("plan-review due: yes", the answer the plan phase is instructed to record) or when, reading the plan, any of these is true: (a) the session-fit answer is "needs multiple sessions"; (b) it names a routed-around contract gap with a ticket identifier (as opposed to an explicit "none identified"); (c) any step relaxes a validation, a contract, or a guard — a widened input, a dropped check, a softened assertion, a gate turned advisory; (d) it touches credential, merge-rule, or dispatch-contract surfaces. **When none of (a)–(d) holds, do NOT emit \`plan-review\`** — fall straight through to the session-fit routing below, exactly as before this gate existed. The step is gated, not universal: it exists to protect the throughput of the work that needs it, so a clean small plan must reach \`implementation\` with no extra dispatch, and a plan's own "plan-review due: no" is taken at face value unless the plan visibly contradicts it (a named routed-around gap sitting beside a "no" is the contradiction to act on).
**Once a plan-review verdict IS on the trail, route on the verdict — and bound the loop at one cycle:**

- **Approve** → route on the session-fit answer exactly as today ("fits one session" → \`implementation\`, "needs multiple sessions" → \`breakdown\`). Do NOT re-emit \`plan-review\` on a plan that already has one; and note that this Approve authorizes implementation only — it is never close-out evidence (see the close-out rules in Step 0 and above).

- **Request Changes / Needs Discussion (the first one)** → \`plan\` — the revision pass, which reads the verdict and answers each finding. This is the single exception to "Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb" above.

- **A SECOND Request Changes / Needs Discussion on the same task** → **stop and escalate to the human edge: recommend \`blocked\`**, naming the findings that survived two passes and what decision is needed. One revision cycle (plan → plan-review → revised plan → plan-review) is *converging*; a second is *looping*, and looping is not fixed by another pass. Do NOT emit a third \`plan-review\`, and do NOT emit another \`plan\`.

context: - **Plan-review prompts** must instruct a fresh-context verifier of the plan's grounding claims, with authority to VERIFY and NOT to redesign: check the plan against its own claims, do not add requirements, and never become a second planner — a different-but-also-reasonable approach is not a finding. The prompt must enumerate all seven checks IN THIS ORDER, each re-running a claim the plan already makes rather than taking the plan's word for a result the agent can reproduce itself: (1) **completeness check** — re-run the surface search independently, searching for the concept or behaviour itself (what a caller or user observes) and not only the symbol the ticket cites, then diff the result against the plan's surface list; a missed sibling is Request Changes unless it is folded in or explicitly marked out-of-scope with a named ticket identifier; (2) **Strategy Framing** — confirm the plan NAMES the root contract gap its chosen strategy routes around, with a ticket identifier or an explicit "none identified", since a bare description is not enough to make the trade-off auditable; (3) **history signal** — re-run \`git log --oneline -15 -- <files in the plan>\` and confirm the constraints those commits surface actually appear in the plan; a file with repeated recent commits over the same code paths whose constraints the plan never mentions is an unverified claim; (4) **session-fit** — test the plan's answer against the catches it names: specific, nameable catches mean "needs multiple sessions" should have been the answer, so a "fits one session" verdict sitting beside them is a contradiction to flag; (5) **relaxation guard** — flag any step that loosens a validation, a contract, or a guard (a widened input, a dropped check, a softened assertion, a gate turned advisory), which is acceptable only where the plan NAMES the adversarial follow-up that re-tightens or bounds it; an unnamed one is Request Changes; (6) **prerequisite-refactor necessity** — confirm any refactor sequenced as a separate blocking subtask names the line in THIS task that consumes it (necessity, not availability), and check the converse too, since a genuinely necessary refactor absorbed into the implementation steps loses the sequencing guarantee and is equally a finding; (7) **source-of-truth re-grounding** — for each data source or upstream contract the plan inherits (a parent design, a prior ticket, house convention, or a prior stage's distilled output), confirm it is authoritative for this use; a lossy, derived, or cached source carrying load-bearing data while the primary source is directly readable is Request Changes, citing the primary source to use instead — primary sources, or derived sources carrying nothing load-bearing, are a valid, common clean result. The prompt must end with an explicit verdict — Approve / Request Changes / Needs Discussion — carrying a one-line justification, the same vocabulary review uses at the other end of the pipeline, and must keep the step WRITE-ONLY: findings and verdict recorded as a comment, with no edits to the plan, no implementing, and no follow-up tickets filed — on Approve hand off to \`implementation\`, otherwise name what the plan must fix and hand it back to \`plan\`. Keep it cheap when clean: a plan surviving all seven checks gets one explicit line ("claims verified; proceed to implementation") and an immediate handoff, so do not manufacture doubt about a well-grounded plan.

laterSites: lib/completion-signals.js::named::readinessCheck: 'Review does not merge or mark Don
context: 'retrospective-audit': {
coreOutcome: 'Claims the deliverable rests on, and the integrity of the tests asserting them, independently checked against the landed code, with findings reported',
signals: [
'Opens from the fact the change is already merged — the landed commit(s)/PR located before auditing anything',
'Claims (in-code comments, PR/task description, summary comment) checked directly against the code at HEAD, not against the author\'s account of them',
'Tests checked for integrity, not just presence — a test passing for a reason unrelated to the behavior it names, a vacuous assertion, or a negative/spy test that never asserts is surfaced',
'Ownership orphans checked — a hazard deferred between this ticket and a sibling it references, unowned by either at HEAD',
'Findings reported as a comment; no status/label/Done change, no merge, and no follow-up ticket filed'

readinessCheck: 'Were the deliverable\'s claims and its tests\' integrity independently checked against the landed code (not the overall correctness CI already covers), with findings reported and no state changed?'

- **Retrospective-audit prompts** must open from the fact that the work is already merged — instruct the agent to locate the landed commit(s)/PR first (e.g. \`git log --grep=<identifier>\`), and must NOT frame the task as a pre-merge review or ask the agent to authorize a merge. They must NOT re-verify overall correctness or re-run the suite to confirm it passes — CI already covers that; the prompt must scope the agent to what an independent post-merge read can see that CI cannot: (1) **audit the claims** — collect every claim the deliverable rests on (in-code comments, the PR/commit description, the task's own description or summary comment) and check each directly against the code at HEAD, not against the author's account of it; (2) **audit test integrity** — for each test guarding a claimed behavior, check whether it actually tests what it claims to (a test passing for a reason unrelated to the behavior it names, a vacuous assertion, a negative/spy test that constructs a forbidden call and never asserts against it), not merely whether it exists or is green; (3) **check for ownership orphans** — a hazard this task's record defers to a sibling ticket while that ticket's own record defers it back here (or elsewhere), a class invisible from inside either ticket alone, so the prompt must instruct the agent to read the referenced sibling's current state directly. The prompt must require findings to be reported as a comment and must explicitly forbid changing status, labels, or any other task state, forbid merging or marking anything Done (already happened — not this step's to redo), and forbid filing follow-up tickets (a finding that warrants one is named in the comment, left for the reader to act on). A finding-free audit is a valid, common result the prompt must allow without manufacturing doubt.

determine the right level from the change itself rather than enforcing a fixed rule; must ALSO instruct the agent to mutation-check the load-bearing tests (LIN-2274) — for at least the new/changed tests that pin this deliverable's own claimed behavior, delete or comment out the code path each one claims to cover and confirm it goes red, since a test that stays green with its own claimed code path removed passes for a reason other than the one it names (e.g. a spy/Proxy never actually wired into the call path under test, or a helper silently slicing the wrong block of a shared file) — record the specific mutation tried and what was observed as a review finding, then revert it, (5) include a class check before approving the close: ask whether the verified work is one instance of a class with unhandled siblings (the same bug or gap under a different name, in a parallel code path, or split across server and client); if so, name the class and record the instances as a review finding rather than expanding the task — a genuinely isolated change is a valid result, (6) **write a \`### What CI Did Not Prove\` ledger** — enumerate every claim the deliverable depends on that the green CI run does NOT exercise (an external contract CI can't reach; a producer that must emit an input this change now consumes; a user-reachable path no test drives; a parallel-surface sibling; anything only a human can confirm), each stated with how it can be discharged; make each item PROPORTIONAL to the change's risk class — an inherently-unprovable-before-merge claim (model/behavioural compliance with a new directive, real-world recurrence of an incident) is a hard close-out gate item only when the change touches runtime logic, a data path, security, or an external contract AND neither named lane below covers it, because NAMING is the price of both lanes and an unnamed monitor or an unnamed rollback does not get either: (i) **name the monitor** — a claim unprovable before merge *in principle* (not merely uncovered by this CI run) is recorded as a post-merge observation that discharges through normal post-merge observation regardless of risk surface, provided the reviewer names the specific monitor that would surface it going wrong (a log or oplog entry, a metric, a path that fails loudly, a routed follow-up that owns the watch), with the misfire guard that a claim a test COULD have proven is an untested claim, not an unprovable one, and stays a gate item; (ii) **name the rollback** — the low-risk lane spans prompt-text / docs / comment-only AND a runtime-logic change that is genuinely reversible, meaning all three of: the reviewer names the rollback (the single commit to revert, or the exact env var / flag and its safe value), the rollback is complete (no migration, no data persisted in the new shape, no third party already consuming the new behaviour), and it needs no coordinated release — data-path, security, and external-contract surfaces are NOT widened into this lane; keying the lane on the risk surface not LOC / t-shirt size / literal file type, and never lowering the floor for risky claims (a claim neither lane covers — one a check or test could have proven, or one on a data, security, or external-contract surface with no complete rollback — stays a hard gate item, and a reviewer's own "no action needed" self-assessment is never a human sign-off); widening the lane never widens the ledger — every claim CI does not exercise is still enumerated, only the discharge route changes; keep it DISTINCT from the class check (class = breadth → follow-up tickets; when CI was genuinely absent and the two-branch substitute stood in for it, its own limits (no independent clean environment, no coverage of later commits, no flake/regression separation beyond this run) are themselves ledger items, not proof the ledger is empty, (7) before the verdict, establish CI status ONCE and boundedly (CI config + \`gh pr checks\`/\`statusCheckRollup\`, one settle if empty; never a poll, never a Monitor on a check set not observed to exist): confirm CI is green on the PR, or, if CI is genuinely absent, that the reviewer independently RE-RAN the substitute — not merely cited the implementer's numbers — and recorded the result; end with an explicit verdict (Approve / Request Changes / Needs Discussion) that is CONDITIONAL on the ledger: a non-empty ledger forces \`Approve — conditional on close-out discharging the ledger\`, never a bare Approve. Review is WRITE-ONLY: it records the ledger and the verdict in the summary comment and must NOT merge, mark the task Done, or file the close-out follow-ups — those irreversible actions hand off to the \`close-out\` step (do not instruct the agent to perform or verify a merge that has not happened; the Approve is its precondition). context: - **Close-out prompts** must gate the irreversible finish on the review ledger: (1) read the review's verdict and any gaps it flagged as unproven by CI from the latest review summary comment; a routed follow-up ticket) or explicitly accepted by a human who names the exact precondition they exercised; (3) treat green CI as evidence for the CI line ONLY — it never discharges a flagged gap, which exists precisely because CI cannot reach it; (3a) honour review's PROPORTIONAL lane — when review recorded an item as a post-merge observation on a low-risk, reversible change (prompt-text / docs / comment-only, no runtime-logic / data-path / security / external-contract surface), that routing to normal post-merge observation (optionally a lightweight monitoring follow-up) IS its discharge under (2)'s cited-follow-up path, so cite it and proceed without a pre-merge human sign-off; two NAMED routes carry the same weight and are accepted the same way, by citing the name review wrote and never one supplied here — a **named monitor** (review judged the claim unprovable before merge in principle and named what would surface it going wrong: a log or oplog entry, a metric, a path that fails loudly, a routed follow-up that owns the watch), whatever the risk surface, and a **named rollback** (review judged a runtime-logic change reversible and named the single commit to revert or the exact env var / flag and its safe value, with no migration, no data persisted in the new shape, no third party already consuming it, and no coordinated release needed); an UNNAMED monitor or an UNNAMED rollback does NOT get the lane — "it can be reverted" or "we will notice" with nothing named is an undischarged item, and the naming belongs to review-authoring time, not here; this lane is keyed on the risk surface and on what review named, does NOT relax the two floors (green CI still never discharges; a risky item still needs cited evidence or a human naming the exact precondition — never the reviewer's own self-assessment), and never waves a genuine gate item through; (4) gate on the review verdict rather than any specific format — when the latest review recorded an Approve (or Approve — conditional), treat the absence of flagged gaps as effectively empty and proceed, noting that in the summary, and treat any caveats a conditional Approve names as gaps to discharge; a recorded, independent review Approve plus a discharged/empty ledger IS the authorization to perform the finish, so a fresh in-session human "go ahead" is not additionally required and that recorded verdict must not be discounted because other context over-asserts authority (this does not lower the floors: green CI never discharges an item, and a risky, undischarged item still needs cited evidence or a human naming the exact precondition); if CI is genuinely absent, confirm the substitute was re-run and recorded on this commit; (6) once every item is discharged or accepted (or the ledger is empty or absent under an Approve) and (CI is green on the exact commit, or CI is genuinely absent and the substitute is recorded on it), perform the irreversible set — merge, verify the change on the landed commit as this session's last step, set the task Done, post the summary, **archive a pre-prune snapshot of the description and then prune superseded stage-artifact sections from it**, and file remaining follow-ups; (3a) honour review's PROPORTIONAL lane — when review recorded an item as a post-merge observation on a low-risk, reversible change (prompt-text / docs / comment-only, no runtime-logic / data-path / security / external-contract surface), that routing to normal post-merge observation (optionally a lightweight monitoring follow-up) IS its discharge under (2)'s cited-follow-up path, so cite it and proceed without a pre-merge human sign-off; two NAMED routes carry the same weight and are accepted the same way, by citing the name review wrote and never one supplied here — a **named monitor** (review judged the claim unprovable before merge in principle and named what would surface it going wrong: a log or oplog entry, a metric, a path that fails loudly, a routed follow-up that owns the watch), whatever the risk surface, and a **named rollback** (review judged a runtime-logic change reversible and named the single commit to revert or the exact env var / flag and its safe value, with no migration, no data persisted in the new shape, no third party already consuming it, and no coordinated release needed); an UNNAMED monitor or an UNNAMED rollback does NOT get the lane — "it can be reverted" or "we will notice" with nothing named is an undischarged item, and the naming belongs to review-authoring time, not here; this lane is keyed on the risk surface and on what review named, does NOT relax the two floors (green CI still never discharges; a risky item still needs cited evidence or a human naming the exact precondition — never the reviewer's own self-assessment), and never waves a genuine gate item through; (4) gate on the review verdict rather than any specific format — when the latest review recorded an Approve (or Approve — conditional), treat the absence of flagged gaps as effectively empty and proceed, noting that in the summary, and treat any caveats a conditional Approve names as gaps to discharge; a recorded, independent review Approve plus a discharged/empty ledger IS the authorization to perform the finish, so a fresh in-session human "go ahead" is not additionally required and that recorded verdict must not be discounted because other context over-asserts authority (this does not lower the floors: green CI never discharges an item, and a risky, undischarged item still needs cited evidence or a human naming the exact precondition); reserve a route back to \`review\` for a task with no review verdict on record; (5) keep it cheap when empty — an explicit "ledger empty", or an Approve with no ledger items, makes close-out a no-op pass-through, so do not manufacture doubt about a self-contained change; (5a) before the merge, establish CI status ONCE and boundedly on the exact commit (CI config + \`gh pr checks\`/\`statusCheckRollup\`, one settle if empty; never a poll, never a Monitor armed on a check set not observed to exist) — if CI exists it must be green; if CI is genuinely absent, confirm the substitute was re-run and recorded on this commit; (6) once every item is discharged or accepted (or the ledger is empty or absent under an Approve) and (CI is green on the exact commit, or CI is genuinely absent and the substitute is recorded on it), perform the irreversible set — merge, verify the change on the landed commit as this session's last step, set the task Done, post the summary, **archive a pre-prune snapshot of the description and then prune superseded stage-artifact sections from it**, and file remaining follow-ups; close the bookkeeping on merge rather than holding the task open for a separate verification pass, and never file a follow-up whose entire content is "confirm the merged change works" — the one bound being a claim that needs real-world elapsed time to show up, which is not verifiable on the landed commit and belongs on (3a)'s named-monitor route instead; (6a) the archive+prune step MUST: archive first via the brief endpoint with its no-generation flag set (zero LLM spend), verify the archive landed via the task-snapshot listing endpoint before editing — if that verification fails, do not prune: record in the summary that the archive could not be confirmed and the prune was skipped, and close the task anyway, since the merge and Done transition have already landed, never holding open, re-routing, or reopening a task whose merge and Done have landed — otherwise rewrite the description removing embedded stage-artifact sections (implementation plan(s) and any plan revisions, research findings, discharged scoping/design sections) and replacing them with a short stub — what shipped, the PR link, whether the plan was implemented as approved or the named deviations, and that full history is preserved in the task snapshots and comment trail; it must NEVER prune the original problem statement, acceptance criteria, reproduction steps, or scope, and it must retain, word for word, the committed session-fit phrase ("fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions") and/or an "Implementation Plan" heading, since deterministic readers key on those exact literals in the description; this step runs only on the all-clear path, never on a cannot-close branch or a task left open with Request Changes / Needs Discussion; (6b) **every follow-up ticket filed above must additionally carry a priority and a type label**, never left at the provider default — derive the priority from the finding's own risk and state that reasoning in one line on the ticket, setting it via the provider-neutral \`priorityLevel\` (ascending, 4 = highest) or the native \`priority\` field, never a hand-invented numeric scale; apply a type label drawn from the workspace's own label catalog (\`GET /api/proxy/labels\`), never a hardcoded vocabulary, and if nothing in that catalog reasonably fits, say so explicitly on the ticket rather than inventing one; both are best-effort — when a provider silently drops priority on write, or offers no usable label catalog, record a one-line note on the ticket instead of retrying or failing the close; this adds metadata only and does not change which follow-ups get filed; (7) always name a next action — when the gate cannot pass, hold the merge, leave the task open, and name \`review\` (to record a verdict) or the \`bug\`/\`plan\`/\`implementation\` that discharges the blocking item.

- **Plan prompts** must include a cross-cutting concerns check: after listing changes, ask whether any requirements share the same code path, state, or interface — and if so, document the expected interaction explicitly. context: - **Review prompts** must: (1) cross-reference the plan's cross-cutting concerns against the implementation steps to identify likely gaps — requirements not addressed in any implementation step are the highest-priority review items, (2) for visual or behavioral changes, instruct the agent to verify directly (take screenshots, run the app, check viewports) — and when a spec or mockup attachment exists for the task, this verification must view that attachment and the actual result side-by-side before judging visual fidelity, never judging fidelity from the result alone, (3) only flag for human testing what the agent genuinely cannot verify (external services, cross-browser, subjective UX), (4) assess whether tests cover the right *level* — for behavior crossing module boundaries, user-facing flows, or integration surfaces, instruct the agent to verify higher-level tests like e2e or integration are present *where appropriate*, not only unit tests with mocks; determine the right level from the change itself rather than enforcing a fixed rule; must ALSO instruct the agent to mutation-check the load-bearing tests (LIN-2274) — for at least the new/changed tests that pin this deliverable's own claimed behavior, delete or comment out the code path each one claims to cover and confirm it goes red, since a test that stays green with its own claimed code path removed passes for a reason other than the one it names (e.g. a spy/Proxy never actually wired into the call path under test, or a helper silently slicing the wrong block of a shared file) — record the specific mutation tried and what was observed as a review finding, then revert it, (5) include a class check before approving the close: ask whether the verified work is one instance of a class with unhandled siblings (the same bug or gap under a different name, in a parallel code path, or split across server and client); if so, name the class and record the instances as a review finding rather than expanding the task — a genuinely isolated change is a valid result, (6) **write a \`### What CI Did Not Prove\` ledger** — enumerate every claim the deliverable depends on that the green CI run does NOT exercise (an external contract CI can't reach; a producer that must emit an input this change now consumes; a user-reachable path no test drives; a parallel-surface sibling; anything only a human can confirm), each stated with how it can be discharged; make each item PROPORTIONAL to the change's risk class — an inherently-unprovable-before-merge claim (model/behavioural compliance with a new directive, real-world recurrence of an incident) is a hard close-out gate item only when the change touches runtime logic, a data path, security, or an external contract AND neither named lane below covers it, because NAMING is the price of both lanes and an unnamed monitor or an unnamed rollback does not get either: (i) **name the monitor** — a claim unprovable before merge *in principle* (not merely uncovered by this CI run) is recorded as a post-merge observation that discharges through normal post-merge observation regardless of risk surface, provided the reviewer names the specific monitor that would surface it going wrong (a log or oplog entry, a metric, a path that fails loudly, a routed follow-up that owns the watch), with the misfire guard that a claim a test COULD have proven is an untested claim, not an unprovable one, and stays a gate item; (ii) **name the rollback** — the low-risk lane spans prompt-text / docs / comment-only AND a runtime-logic change that is genuinely reversible, meaning all three of: the reviewer names the rollback (the single commit to revert, or the exact env var / flag and its safe value), the rollback is complete (no migration, no data persisted in the new shape, no third party already consuming the new behaviour), and it needs no coordinated release — data-path, security, and external-contract surfaces are NOT widened into this lane; context: - **Research prompts** must end with a Surface Assessment gated on necessity, not availability: the question is not "would a refactor make this land better?" (on most code something could be cleaner) but "is the feature's shape demanding a structural change?" — implementing cleanly would mean fighting the current structure. A "refactor required" verdict must pass two evidence tests, each answered by citing lines: the **consumer test** (cite the line in THIS task's implementation that calls the new seam — no citation means speculation, which belongs with its future consumer, not ahead of it) and the **who-pays test** (every consumer the refactor touches is either a beneficiary — simpler, corrected, or unchanged — or a bystander paying a named tax; an unjustified bystander tax means scope it down; a small named tax buying a large simplification must be argued explicitly). Size is not a rejection criterion — a demanded refactor that does not fit the session is sequenced, not shrunk. Format: "Surface Assessment: [lands cleanly] / [refactor required: describe the minimal scoped change — consumer: where this task calls it] / [improvement noticed, not required: land inline/scoped — no separate subtask]". The answer must be explicit — not implied — so the plan step can act on it. Research prompts must also search wider than nearby code — prior investigations or runs of the same subsystem and prior diverging episodes (seed from both the technical lead and the meta-pattern, "this class of problem, last time the decisive experiment was X"), not only related fixes — and must pin the measurement: if the work will be judged by a metric or signal, confirm it actually tracks the real outcome before optimizing against it; a measurement that can read green while the outcome is wrong (or red while it is right) must be validated or replaced first (a measurement that genuinely tracks the outcome is a valid answer and must be stated explicitly). Research prompts must also require an explicit Audit the Layers pass before recommending: enumerate every layer the change touches — every part, seam, or module it must stay consistent with — searching for the concept (what a caller or user observes), not only the symbol the ticket cites, since the same behaviour is often represented under a different name, in a parallel code path, split across server and client, mirrored in a sibling provider/feature, or restated in a published contract. For each layer, instruct the consumer to brief how it is done here today (its patterns, conventions, and normalisations, and what a change must keep consistent) AND to cite a source for each claim — a file:line, a doc path, or a commit — so the brief is verified, not assumed; an uncited claim is a guess. Completion is measured by coverage, not speed — being exhaustive costs the same human attention. As part of each layer's brief, enumerate what the change must hold true against in the existing system — what it must reuse rather than duplicate, stay consistent with across sibling surfaces, keep in sync across sources of truth, preserve behaviourally, and recover from on failure — citing the specific existing thing for each and how the approach honours it. These axes are seed examples, not a fixed checklist (the decisive axis may be concurrency, auth scoping, cache invalidation, rate limits, …); the consumer derives the axes the task actually has, and the target is completeness of reasoning, not a longer list. Research prompts must then include an adversarial self-review pass that CLOSES the layer set — instruct the agent to attack its own audit: what existing structure, sibling surface, sync obligation, failure path, or prior behaviour did it not check, and what did it assert without verifying; it must state the layer set as complete and back it by showing the search that would have surfaced a missed sibling and what it returned, resolving or recording what that turns up before recommending. And the Surface Assessment must treat introducing a second representation of something already modelled (a parallel type/table/state/source of truth for existing data) as a "refactor required" signal — reuse or extend the existing model — not a clean landing. All of this applies when the change touches shared structure, multiple surfaces, or already-modelled data; a genuinely small or single-surface change (a typo, a constant, a one-file edit) records the file and the fix, skips the layer audit and adversarial passes, and does not pay the obligation tax. context: '- **Unprovable in principle → name the monitor.** A claim that cannot be proven before merge *at all* — not merely one this CI run happens not to cover — is recorded as a **post-merge observation** and discharges through normal post-merge observation **regardless of risk surface**, provided you name the specific monitor that would surface it going wrong: a log or oplog entry, a metric, or a path that fails loudly. A monitor is a thing that **fires**, and a routed follow-up ticket is not one — it may be cited *beside* the monitor to record who holds the watch, never *instead* of it. If no monitor can be named, it stays a hard gate item. *Misfire guard — write the line:* before an item takes this lane, write one line naming why no check short of production could prove the claim; an entry with no such line does not take the lane, and close-out rejects it as undischarged. The guard is a step, not a caveat: a claim a test COULD have proven is not unprovable-in-principle — it is an untested claim, it stays a gate item, and it usually means **Request Changes**. Naming the monitor is the price of the lane, not a formality.',

context: 'Before the verdict, write the handoff ledger — the artifact the `close-out` step consumes. Enumerate every claim the deliverable depends on that the green CI run does NOT actually exercise. Common kinds (illustrative, not a checklist): an external contract or API behaviour CI cannot reach; a *producer* that must emit an input this change now *consumes*; a user-reachable entry path no automated test drives; a sibling on a parallel surface; or anything only a human can confirm. For each item, mark it **inside** or **outside** the ticket\'s bounded classes (see Inside or Outside the Ticket\'s Scope above) and state how it can be discharged: an **inside** item — this ticket\'s own unfinished scope — by a real-world check or a manual repro naming its **exact distinguishing precondition**; filing a ticket for it is never a discharge, since it belongs to this ticket, not a neighbour\'s. An **outside** item — a genuinely different kind of problem — by a routed follow-up ticket that states the problem on its own terms.',

context: **Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. A subtask whose own description carries such a copied approved-parent-plan slice with a committed session-fit answer is itself a complete plan for the purposes of this rule — treat it as settled prep even though the \`plan\` step never literally ran on this specific ticket; do not recommend \`plan\` merely because this ticket has no \`plan\`-session history of its own. **This settled-prep read does NOT apply when the child's copied slice visibly diverges from what the cited approving verdict approved** — a diverged slice is not settled prep; fall through to the plan-review gate immediately below, which re-derives on that same divergence. context: **Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. context: **Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. A subtask whose own description carries such a copied approved-parent-plan slice with a committed session-fit answer is itself a complete plan for the purposes of this rule — treat it as settled prep even though the \`plan\` step never literally ran on this specific ticket; do not recommend \`plan\` merely because this ticket has no \`plan\`-session history of its own. **This settled-prep read does NOT apply when the child's copied slice visibly diverges from what the cited approving verdict approved** — a diverged slice is not settled prep; fall through to the plan-review gate immediately below, which re-derives on that same divergence. ONE exception, and only one: a \`plan-review\` that recorded **Request Changes** or **Needs Discussion** makes the plan's deliverable un-settled again, so the revision pass it names IS a \`plan\` that is still owed — see the plan-review gate immediately below, which bounds it to a single cycle.

context: **Completed prep ⇒ never re-emit the prep verb.** The mirror of the rule above: a prep verb (\`research\`/\`plan\`) is owed only when its deliverable does NOT already exist and settle in the artifacts — never re-recommend a preparation stage whose work is already complete. A ticket whose description already carries a complete plan (surfaces enumerated, an approach, and a committed session-fit answer of "fits one session" / "needs multiple sessions"), and/or a breakdown-shaped plan comment, AND has no child issues yet → the plan stage is DONE: route on its session-fit answer to \`breakdown\` (needs multiple sessions) or \`implementation\` (fits one session), NEVER another \`plan\`. Weigh what the artifacts already DELIVER — not the node still being In Progress, and NOT the plan's own self-referential prose: a settled plan that names its own "recommended next action" as "create the Phase A subtask" / "file the … subtask" / "a plan ticket that sequences …" is describing a \`breakdown\` (decompose the finished plan into subtasks), not asking for more planning — that prose is the plan's output, not evidence planning is still owed. (Same artifact-completeness read as the Step-2 divergence veto, opposite pole: settled-prep vs not-yet-started-prep.) This composes with the no-committed-scope rule as its mirror — scope ABSENT resolves DOWN to \`plan\`/\`research\`; a settled prep deliverable PRESENT resolves UP to \`breakdown\`/\`implementation\` — and it overrides neither opposite pole: a genuinely thin or absent plan still → \`plan\`; a fresh ticket whose underlying knowledge is ungathered still → \`research\`; scope-absent still never routes to \`implement\`. - **Plan-review prompts** must instruct a fresh-context verifier of the plan's grounding claims to check the plan against its own claims, adding no requirements of its own (code adds the verify-not-redesign line). The prompt must enumerate all seven checks IN THIS ORDER, each re-running a claim the plan already makes rather than taking the plan's word for a result the agent can reproduce itself: (1) **completeness check — argue the class, not the member** — where the plan named a class and how it bounded it, re-derive that bound (re-run the query it cites at the sha it names, or redo the reasoning) and diff the result against the members the plan handled, which is the mechanical half where a query exists (either they match or the difference is the finding); if a member the plan lacks turns up, the verdict does not stop at the member — it must say what class the member belongs to, how the verifier bounded that class, and every other member that bounding found, so one round covers the whole class; only where the plan cites no bound for a class it claims to cover does the verifier fall back to searching independently for the concept or behaviour itself (what a caller or user observes) rather than only the symbol the ticket cites, then diffing against the plan's surface list; a missed class is Request Changes unless it is folded in or explicitly marked out-of-scope with a named ticket identifier — a plan is never sent back for a missing member inside a class already correctly bounded, only for a missing or wrongly-bounded class. The prompt must instruct that a verifier who believes the bounding is wrong argues about the BOUND — proposing the class, the query or reasoning they would use instead, and showing what it finds — because two people disagreeing about a bound converge once one of them runs it, whereas discovering members one at a time does not. It must also instruct that a plan declaring a class un-sweepable is not thereby incomplete: check the REASON rather than the absence (destinations of new or moved code cannot be swept from code that does not exist; a class whose population is production data needs a corpus query), treat a sound reason plus a stated alternative bound as a clean pass, and demand a sweep only where the verifier can name the query that would produce one — and then name it; (2) **Strategy Framing** — confirm the plan NAMES the root contract gap its chosen strategy routes around, with a ticket identifier or an explicit "none identified", since a bare description is not enough to make the trade-off auditable, and that routing around a cause this task could fix carries a reason it cannot be fixed here, else Request Changes; (3) **history signal** — re-run \`git log --oneline -15 -- <files in the plan>\` and confirm the constraints those commits surface actually appear in the plan; a file with repeated recent commits over the same code paths whose constraints the plan never mentions is an unverified claim; (4) **session-fit** — test the plan's answer against the catches it names: specific, nameable catches mean "needs multiple sessions" should have been the answer, so a "fits one session" verdict sitting beside them is a contradiction to flag; (5) **relaxation guard** — flag any step that loosens a validation, a contract, or a guard (a widened input, a dropped check, a softened assertion, a gate turned advisory), which is acceptable only where the plan NAMES the adversarial follow-up that re-tightens or bounds it; an unnamed one is Request Changes; (6) **prerequisite-refactor necessity** — confirm any refactor sequenced as a separate blocking subtask names the line in THIS task that consumes it (necessity, not availability), and check the converse too, since a genuinely necessary refactor absorbed into the implementation steps loses the sequencing guarantee and is equally a finding; (2) **Strategy Framing** — confirm the plan NAMES the root contract gap its chosen strategy routes around, with a ticket identifier or an explicit "none identified", since a bare description is not enough to make the trade-off auditable, and that routing around a cause this task could fix carries a reason it cannot be fixed here, else Request Changes; (3) **history signal** — re-run \`git log --oneline -15 -- <files in the plan>\` and confirm the constraints those commits surface actually appear in the plan; a file with repeated recent commits over the same code paths whose constraints the plan never mentions is an unverified claim; (4) **session-fit** — test the plan's answer against the catches it names: specific, nameable catches mean "needs multiple sessions" should have been the answer, so a "fits one session" verdict sitting beside them is a contradiction to flag; (5) **relaxation guard** — flag any step that loosens a validation, a contract, or a guard (a widened input, a dropped check, a softened assertion, a gate turned advisory), which is acceptable only where the plan NAMES the adversarial follow-up that re-tightens or bounds it; an unnamed one is Request Changes; (6) **prerequisite-refactor necessity** — confirm any refactor sequenced as a separate blocking subtask names the line in THIS task that consumes it (necessity, not availability), and check the converse too, since a genuinely necessary refactor absorbed into the implementation steps loses the sequencing guarantee and is equally a finding; (7) **source-of-truth re-grounding** — for each data source or upstream contract the plan inherits (a parent design, a prior ticket, house convention, or a prior stage's distilled output), confirm it is authoritative for this use; a lossy, derived, or cached source carrying load-bearing data while the primary source is directly readable is Request Changes, citing the primary source to use instead — primary sources, or derived sources carrying nothing load-bearing, are a valid, common clean result. The prompt must end with an explicit verdict — Approve / Request Changes / Needs Discussion — carrying a one-line justification, the same vocabulary review uses at the other end of the pipeline, and must keep the step WRITE-ONLY: findings and verdict recorded as a comment, with no edits to the plan, no implementing, and no follow-up tickets filed — on Approve hand off to \`implementation\`, otherwise name what the plan must fix and hand it back to \`plan\`. Keep it cheap when clean: a plan surviving all seven checks gets one explicit line ("claims verified; proceed to implementation") and an immediate handoff, so do not manufacture doubt about a well-grounded plan.
